tells: 'it is the law lived from the inside' — a tidy aphorism closing a thought; Author A explains with a concrete image (the lamp, the rusted machine) rather than a polished antithesis
'a reader should feel able to say what ʿirfan is and is not' — presumes what the reader will feel; Author A states what the Qur'an or a scholar says and leaves the reader alone
'small, practical steps for bringing this into daily life' — self-help register; Author A's diction is plainer and never sells the book's usefulness
Quotation named and integrated mid-sentence ('an ʿarif is, in Sheikh Bahmanpour's words, "someone who knows"'), plain diction, second paragraph picks up 'knowing' from the first

Each paragraph opens on the last point ('Knowledge by presence is complete...'), concrete everyday examples (hunger, pain, anxiety), semicolon antithesis 'the cause is not the feeling' matches 'we are failing to receive them'
'has called for some editorial adaptation' — abstract prefatory jargon; Author A would say what was changed
'adds context and explanation to support its main arguments' — describes the book in generic terms; Author A never talks about the book's method in the abstract
'Every source is given in a footnote, for readers who want to go further' — a service note to the reader; Author A does not address the reader's convenience

'a prayer many of us recite' mirrors 'a verse often recited at weddings, one most of us know'; inclusive 'we' and the move from accepted words to unpractised meaning matches the reference's 'accepting that a sign exists is not the same as perceiving it'

Quotation introduced with speaker and explained ('There is, he writes, "no niggardliness...", which give of their nature'); 'Whatever stands between the heart and the light stands on our side' restates the reference's 'the fault is on our side' in the same plain register
'remain an ongoing conversation among our ʿulamaʾ' — abstract, slightly academic phrasing; Author A would write 'our scholars still disagree about'
'Three guiding principles frame the discussions in the chapters that follow' — 'frame the discussions' is managerial diction Author A never uses
'this book presents each view with neutrality' — self-description of method; Author A simply presents the views
'Then: "These are shirk."' — a one-word fragment and colon staged for dramatic effect; Author A would write 'He then calls these shirk' and explain
'is the gravest charge in Islam' — a weighty summary line; Author A keeps to what the speaker said

'Let's start with the order in which the prayers ask' echoes 'Let's start with two claims'; quotation given with speaker then unpacked ('In the heart, he answers, it is'), and a back-reference to Chapter One's sensitivity to signs

Opens by picking up the previous point ('If the faculty can be repaired, there should be people in whom it already works'); the red-light style explanation of the verse ('a name means little to a person who does not know whom it names')

Quotations named, integrated and then explained in the author's own words ('A result in the laboratory is known because it has been observed, not because it has been deduced'), paralleling the lamp explanation in the reference

Dense 'he says' attribution with plain paraphrase, inclusive 'people like us', and the semicolon antithesis 'the first three ranks, he says, are beyond us; the fourth is a doorway' match the reference's habits
'And it ends not in withdrawal from the world but in return' — sentence opened with 'And' in an anaphoric run of short declaratives; Author A never opens with 'And' or builds rhetorical crescendos
'some of the words you'll meet' — contraction and direct 'you'; Author A writes 'we' and 'most of us', never 'you'
'a guide to beginning the journey that strives for brevity and clarity' — the book praising itself; Author A never describes the book's virtues
'Additional call-out sections are spread throughout with helpful context' — 'helpful' is blurb language

'The scholars differ in emphasis but agree that powers are not the aim. Sheikh Bahmanpour calls such powers shirk. Mutahhari explains why...' — a closing paragraph that only recaps what was just said; Author A's synthesis sentences move the argument on ('Placing the fault in the receiver has two consequences')

'Mutahhari explains why seeking them would be so: the goal has become something other than God' — bare surname and a colon-stacked summary clause; Author A writes 'Murtada Mutahhari' and explains in a full sentence

'The scholars speak of how far a reciter reaches; the Sheikh speaks of who may begin' matches the reference's balanced semicolon antithesis ('God is not withholding signs; we are failing to receive them'); second paragraph picks up 'access to these words' from the first
Verse-then-comment rhythm identical to the reference's Surah al-Rum sequence, each verse introduced by who it is promised to and followed by Sheikh Bahmanpour's reading in plain words

'Let's take them in turn' matches the reference's 'Let's start'; 'The eyes in our heads work and still we miss the signs, because the faculty behind them is blind' restates the cattle passage in the same plain register
'Most of us fear Allah's punishment' echoes 'Most of us see only the lamp'; verses introduced by naming the surah and who it describes, then one short explanatory sentence
